description.en: The band standing alternate chest press is performed with a band anchored behind you while pressing one handle at a time forward to chest height. Alternating arms forces the core to resist rotation. It builds chest, front delt, and trunk stability in one move.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height behind you.
Stand facing away from the anchor with a handle in each hand.
Hold the handles at chest level with elbows tucked.
Step forward to add tension to the band.
Brace your core hard against rotation.
Press one handle straight forward to full extension.
Squeeze the chest at the end of the press.
Return slowly and alternate sides.
Builds chest strength
Trains anti-rotation core stability
Single-arm work fixes imbalances
No bench required
Easy to set up at home
Builds functional pressing strength

description.en: The band straight-arm pulldown mimics the cable straight-arm pulldown using a resistance band anchored overhead. You stand facing the anchor and pull both ends of the band down to your thighs with straight arms, isolating the lats without bicep involvement.

en: Anchor a resistance band at a high point above head height.
Face the anchor. Grip both ends of the band with palms down, arms extended forward at chest height.
Step back until the band is taut.
Hinge slightly at the hips. Keep your arms straight (slight elbow bend only).
Pull the band down toward your thighs in an arc using only your lats.
Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom when your hands reach your thighs.
Slowly let the band return to the start over two seconds.
Keep your arms straight throughout — the movement comes from your shoulders.
Isolates the lats without bicep involvement
Constant band tension throughout
Highly portable
Useful when no cable machine is available
Excellent lat activation exercise
Easy to scale by band thickness

description.en: The barbell bench press with 3 boards places 3 wooden boards on the chest, raising the bottom position of the press. The shorter range of motion lets you handle more weight than a full bench press, building lockout strength and triceps power. More boards means a shorter range and heavier loading.

en: Have a training partner hold 3 boards on your chest, or strap them onto your shirt.
Lie on a flat bench under the loaded barbell.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar with control until it touches the top board.
Press the bar back up explosively, locking out at the top.
Re-rack the bar carefully when finished.
Partial range allows heavier loads than full bench
Builds lockout and triceps strength
Different board heights target different sticking points
Reduces stress on the shoulders
Common method in powerlifting accessory work
Helps overcome bench press plateaus

description.en: The barbell bent-arm pullover keeps the elbows significantly bent (about 90 degrees) throughout the pullover arc. The bent-arm position shortens the lever arm, allowing heavier loading, and shifts more emphasis to the chest compared to the straight-arm version which targets the lats more.

en: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a barbell at your chest with elbows bent at 90 degrees.
Keep your elbows bent at roughly 90 degrees throughout.
Arc the bar behind your head by hinging at the shoulders. Elbows stay bent.
Lower until you feel a stretch in your chest and lats.
Pull the bar back over to your chest, maintaining the bent-arm position.
Squeeze your chest at the top.
Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
The bent arms allow heavier loading than straight-arm pullovers.
Shifts emphasis toward the chest
Allows heavier loading than straight-arm version
Builds chest and lat size
Different stimulus from standard pullover
Old-school bodybuilding exercise
Builds ribcage expansion (traditional belief)

description.en: The barbell hack squat is an old-school standing quad exercise where the barbell is held behind the body with arms straight, starting on the floor behind your heels. Named after George Hackenschmidt, the wrestler who popularized it, the lift loads the quads heavily through a unique posterior-loaded squat pattern. It is more knee-dominant than a traditional deadlift and more posterior-loaded than a squat.

en: Stand in front of a loaded barbell so the bar is on the floor directly behind your heels.
Squat down and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart, palms facing your body.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart with toes slightly turned out. Lift your chest and brace your core.
Drive through your feet and stand straight up, lifting the bar off the floor while keeping it in contact with your glutes and hamstrings on the way up.
Stand tall at the top with the bar held behind your thighs and arms straight.
Lower the bar by sitting back and bending the knees, keeping the bar tracking close to your body.
Touch the bar lightly to the floor (or stop just above) and drive back up for the next rep.
The lift is unusual and feels awkward at first — start light and master the groove before loading heavily.
Hits the quadriceps from a unique angle that traditional squats and lunges miss
Builds grip and forearm strength through the loaded hold
Develops posterior-chain coordination similar to a Romanian deadlift
Knee-friendly compared to many heavy quad-dominant lifts
Requires no rack or special equipment — just a barbell
Historically validated and used by some of the strongest lifters of the early 20th century

description.en: The barbell overhead shrug holds a barbell locked out overhead with a wide snatch grip and performs shrugging motions — elevating and depressing the shoulders. It builds upper trap strength in the overhead position and improves overhead stability for snatches.

en: Press or snatch a barbell overhead with a wide grip. Lock out fully.
Stand tall with the bar overhead.
Without bending your elbows, shrug your shoulders up toward your ears.
Squeeze your upper traps at the top.
Lower your shoulders back to neutral.
Continue for the desired reps.
Use light to moderate weight.
This builds the overhead shrug position used in snatch receiving.
Builds upper trap strength in overhead position
Improves overhead stability for snatches
Develops scapular elevation strength
Useful Olympic lifting accessory
Unique shrug variation
Trains trap function at extended overhead range

description.en: The barbell pin front squat is a front squat variation where each rep starts from pins set at parallel or below. Eliminating the stretch reflex forces pure concentric strength out of the bottom of the front squat, building drive from the hardest position of the lift.

en: Set safety pins in a power rack at parallel-squat depth.
Position the barbell on the pins and load it.
Step under the bar and set it across your front shoulders in a clean rack grip.
Stand into a quarter squat to unrack the bar from the pins.
Lower yourself back down until the bar settles on the pins again.
Pause briefly with the bar resting on the pins.
Drive up explosively from the dead stop, keeping your elbows high.
Lock out at the top with chest tall, then lower for the next rep.
Builds dead-stop concentric strength
Eliminates the stretch reflex
Trains the front squat from its weakest point
Useful for breaking through front squat sticking points
Forces strict bracing and form
Strong carryover to clean recoveries

description.en: The barbell seated overhead triceps extension is an isolation exercise performed seated on a bench with back support, lowering a barbell behind your head by bending at the elbows. The seated position eliminates core and lower-back demand while providing back support, allowing you to focus entirely on stretching and contracting the triceps. Use an EZ bar for wrist comfort if needed.

en: Sit on a bench with back support set upright (90 degrees). Grip a barbell with an overhand grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Press the barbell overhead until your arms are fully extended.
Pull your shoulders down and back into the pad. Brace your core. Keep your ribs down.
Slowly lower the barbell behind your head by bending only at the elbows. Keep your upper arms pointing straight up.
Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your triceps. The bar should end just behind your head.
Extend your arms back up to the overhead lockout by contracting your triceps.
Maintain the upper arm position throughout. Do not let your elbows flare out or drift forward.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight and strict form.
Back support eliminates core and lower-back demand
Places the long head under maximum stretch
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell versions
Loaded stretch position drives effective muscle growth
Safer than standing overhead extensions for many lifters
Easy to load progressively over time

description.en: The barbell spider curl is a strict bicep isolation exercise performed lying chest-down on an incline bench with arms hanging straight down. The locked-forward arm position eliminates body english and isolates the biceps better than any standing curl variation. The position also targets the bicep peak.

en: Set an adjustable bench to roughly 45 degrees. Lie face down on it with chest pressed against the pad.
Hold a barbell with both hands using an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Let the barbell hang straight down with arms fully extended.
Brace your core. Press your chest into the pad.
Curl the barbell up by bending at the elbows. Keep your upper arms perpendicular to the floor.
Continue curling until your forearms touch your biceps or come close.
Squeeze your biceps hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control over two to three seconds.
Strict bicep isolation
Eliminates body english entirely
Targets the bicep peak
Builds bicep size and shape
Excellent for breaking through curl plateaus
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The barbell staggered stance hip thrust uses a staggered foot position with one foot forward and one back. Most of the work falls on the front working leg while the back foot provides light balance. It is a stepping stone between standard hip thrusts and full single-leg hip thrusts that allows heavier loading.

en: Set up with upper back against a bench, barbell across your hips.
Plant your right foot flat on the floor with knee bent.
Place your left heel lightly on the floor in front, with toe up.
Most of the work should fall on the right foot.
Brace your core and pin your shoulders to the bench.
Drive your right hip up by squeezing your right glute hard.
Continue lifting until your hip is fully extended.
Lower your hip back down with control. Complete reps, switch sides.
Single-leg bias with two-leg support
Stepping stone to full single-leg hip thrust
Allows heavier loading than full single-leg version
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong glute development
Useful for progressing single-leg work

description.en: The barbell standing wrist reverse curl is a forearm extensor exercise performed standing with the bar held in front of the thighs with an overhand grip. By extending the wrists upward against the bar weight, you train the forearm extensors directly. It builds the back of the forearm for full arm thickness.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a barbell at thigh level with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Allow the bar to rest against the front of your thighs.
Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides.
Lower the bar by extending your wrists down toward the floor.
Allow the bar to roll back through your fingers slightly at the bottom.
Curl the bar back up by extending your wrists upward.
Squeeze the forearm extensors at the top of the curl.
Trains forearm extensors directly
Builds back of forearm for arm thickness
Strict isolation
Allows progressive loading
Improves wrist strength
Useful for athletes who need strong forearms

description.en: The bottle weighted kneeling squat performs a kneeling squat (sitting back onto the heels and rising back up) while holding a water jug or weighted bottle at the chest. The kneeling pattern eliminates quad contribution and forces the glutes to do most of the work. It is a strong home-friendly glute exercise.

en: Kneel on the floor with knees padded and hip-width apart.
Hold a weighted bottle at chest level.
Stand tall on your knees with hips fully extended.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Sit your hips back to lower your butt toward your heels.
Continue until your butt nearly touches your heels.
Drive your hips forward to return to the upright kneeling position.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Glute-focused training
Eliminates quad dominance
No gym equipment required
Useful for home training
Builds glute strength
Easy to scale by changing bottle weight

description.en: The bottle weighted straight legs deadlift is a stiff legged deadlift variation using water bottles for at-home training. The lifter holds bottles in each hand and hinges at the hips with the legs straight. The straight leg position loads the hamstrings hard.

en: Hold a filled water bottle in each hand at the sides.
Stand tall with feet hip width apart.
Set a slight soft bend in the knees.
Brace your core and set the chest tall.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Lower the bottles down the front of the legs.
Continue until you feel a strong stretch in the hamstrings.
Drive the hips forward to stand back up squeezing the glutes.
Strong hamstring builder
Builds the glutes
Trains the hip hinge
Easy at-home alternative
Builds the posterior chain
No gym needed

description.en: The burpee is a full-body bodyweight conditioning exercise that combines a squat, plank, push-up, and vertical jump into one continuous movement. It elevates the heart rate quickly, builds muscular endurance across the entire body, and requires no equipment, making it a staple of high-intensity interval training and metabolic conditioning workouts.

en: Start standing with feet shoulder-width apart and arms at your sides.
Squat down and place your hands on the floor in front of your feet, roughly shoulder-width apart.
Jump or step both feet back into a high plank position with your body forming a straight line from head to heels.
Perform a full push-up by lowering your chest to the floor, then pressing back up to the plank position. Keep your core braced and your hips level.
Jump or step your feet forward to land just outside your hands, returning to a low squat position.
Drive through your heels and explode upward into a vertical jump, reaching your arms overhead.
Land softly with your knees slightly bent, then immediately drop into the next rep. Keep moving for the prescribed time or rep count.
Trains cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance simultaneously
Works the entire body: legs, chest, shoulders, triceps, and core in every rep
Burns a high number of calories per minute
Requires no equipment and minimal space
Easily scaled up or down by adjusting speed, push-up depth, or jump height
Builds mental toughness through sustained high-intensity effort

description.en: The cable horizontal Pallof press is the gold-standard anti-rotation core exercise. You stand sideways to a cable set at chest height, hold the handle at your chest, and press it straight forward. The cable tries to rotate your torso — you resist. It builds deep core anti-rotation strength.

en: Set a cable pulley to chest height. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with both hands at your chest.
Step away from the cable until there is tension.
Brace your core hard. Maintain square hips and shoulders.
Press the handle straight forward by extending your arms.
The cable pulls you to rotate — resist and maintain square position.
Hold at full extension for 2 to 3 seconds.
Pull the handle back to your chest. Repeat 10 to 12 reps per side.
Gold-standard anti-rotation core exercise
Builds deep core stability
Develops oblique and TVA strength
Easy to load progressively
Functional core training
Carries over to all rotational sports

description.en: The cable incline close grip curl is performed lying back on an incline bench with a low cable. Using a close grip on the cable attachment, you curl with the arms hanging behind the body. The combination of incline stretch and close grip emphasizes the long head of the biceps for the bicep peak.

en: Set an incline bench facing away from a low cable station.
Attach a short bar or rope to a low cable pulley.
Lie back on the incline bench with the cable behind you.
Grip the attachment with a close underhand grip.
Allow your arms to hang behind your body in a fully stretched position.
Pin your shoulders back against the bench.
Curl the attachment up by bending only at the elbows.
Squeeze your biceps at the top, then lower with control to the stretched position.
Targets long head of biceps
Strong stretch from incline angle
Close grip emphasizes outer arm
Constant cable tension
Useful for hypertrophy training
Builds bicep peak

description.en: The cable kneeling twist is performed in a tall kneeling position holding a cable handle. By rotating the torso while gripping the cable, you train rotational core strength with constant tension. The kneeling position eliminates leg drive and isolates the core through the rotation.

en: Set a cable to chest height with a single handle.
Kneel sideways to the cable station with both knees on the floor.
Grip the handle with both hands at chest level.
Step away from the anchor to create cable tension.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to lock the hips.
Rotate your torso away from the cable, pulling the handle across your body.
Continue rotating until your arms are extended on the far side.
Slowly return to the starting position with control. Complete reps, switch sides.
Trains rotational core strength
Constant cable tension through the rotation
Kneeling position eliminates leg drive
Strong oblique engagement
Useful for athletes needing rotational power
Easy to scale by changing cable resistance

description.en: The cable lying shrug is performed lying face down on a flat or incline bench with cables running from a low pulley up to handles at your shoulders. The lying position changes the angle of pull from a standard standing shrug, emphasizing the middle and lower traps. The cables provide constant tension throughout the range.

en: Set up a flat or incline bench between two cable stations.
Attach D-handles to low pulleys on each side.
Lie face down on the bench with arms hanging off the sides.
Grip a handle in each hand with palms facing each other.
Allow your arms to hang down with cable tension active.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Shrug your shoulder blades back and together as if pinning them to your spine.
Hold the squeeze for one count, then lower with control.
Constant cable tension through the range
Targets middle and lower trap fibers
Different stimulus than standing shrugs
Improves scapular control
Helps with posture
Strong for full trap development

description.en: The cable rope incline bench row is a back exercise performed lying face down on an incline bench, pulling a rope handle from a low cable pulley. The chest support eliminates body english for strict back isolation, and the rope allows a neutral grip and wider range of motion.

en: Set an incline bench (30 to 45 degrees) facing a low cable pulley. Attach a rope handle.
Lie face down on the bench. Grip the rope with both hands.
Start with arms extended toward the cable, chest on the bench.
Row the rope toward your lower chest by driving your elbows back and flaring the rope ends.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
The chest support eliminates all momentum.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Strict back isolation from chest support
Rope allows neutral grip and wider motion
Easy on the lower back
Constant cable tension throughout
Easy to load progressively
Excellent for back hypertrophy

description.en: The cable shrug is a trap isolation exercise performed at a low cable pulley with a straight bar or rope attachment. The cable provides constant tension throughout the entire range of motion, including the top contraction and bottom stretch where free weights lose resistance. It is an excellent variation for building upper trap size with strict form.

en: Attach a straight bar to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine with feet hip-width apart.
Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Stand tall and step back slightly so the cable is under tension.
Let the bar hang at arm’s length in front of your thighs. Keep your arms completely straight throughout.
Pull your shoulders back and brace your core.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can. Do not bend at the elbows.
Squeeze your traps hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not roll your shoulders.
Lower your shoulders under control. Maintain cable tension throughout — do not let the weight stack touch down.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion
Better resistance at the top contraction than free-weight shrugs
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Excellent for high-rep trap volume
Easier to maintain strict form than barbell or dumbbell shrugs
Trains grip and forearm strength

description.en: The ceiling look stretch is a simple neck stretch performed by gently tilting the head back to look at the ceiling. It stretches the sternocleidomastoid, the front of the neck, and the muscles under the chin. It is useful for relieving forward-head posture from desk work and screen time.

en: Stand or sit with your back tall and shoulders relaxed.
Keep your chest up and shoulders pulled back.
Slowly tilt your head back to look up at the ceiling.
Continue tilting until you feel a gentle stretch on the front of your neck.
Avoid forcing the stretch or jamming the neck back.
Hold the position and breathe normally.
Slowly return your head to the neutral position.
Repeat for several gentle reps.
Stretches the front of the neck
Counteracts forward-head posture
Useful for desk workers
Relieves neck tightness
Improves neck mobility

description.en: The crunch with medicine ball is a loaded crunch variation where you hold a medicine ball at your chest or extended overhead during the crunch. The added weight provides progressive overload to standard crunches, making them more demanding for ab strength development.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor.
Hold a medicine ball with both hands at your chest or extended above your chest.
Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor.
Curl your torso up toward your knees, lifting your shoulders off the floor.
Continue curling until your shoulder blades clear the floor.
Squeeze your abs hard at the top.
Lower under control over two seconds. Stop just before your shoulders touch the floor.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. For more difficulty, hold the ball overhead.
Adds progressive load to crunches
Builds ab strength beyond bodyweight
Easy to scale by ball weight or ball position
Useful when sit-ups are too easy
No bench needed
Effective home ab exercise

description.en: The depth jump to hurdle hop is an advanced plyometric combination where you drop from a box, land, and immediately hop over a series of hurdles. The depth jump teaches reactive force absorption while the hurdle hops train consecutive explosive jumping. It is used for sport-specific power training.

en: Set up a low box (12 to 18 inches) with a series of low hurdles (6 to 12 inches) in front, spaced 2 to 4 feet apart.
Stand on top of the box. Step off (do not jump down).
Land softly on both feet with bent knees just in front of the first hurdle.
Immediately upon landing, explode forward and up to clear the first hurdle.
Land on the other side and immediately hop the next hurdle.
Continue hopping consecutively over all hurdles. Each landing should immediately produce the next jump.
Focus on minimal ground contact time — bounce off the floor quickly.
Perform 4 to 6 reps per set with full recovery.
Elite reactive power development
Trains stretch-shortening cycle
Builds consecutive explosive jumping
Carries over to sport performance
Develops fast-twitch fiber recruitment
Useful for advanced athletes

description.en: The dumbbell alternate Arnold press is the classic Arnold press performed one arm at a time. While one dumbbell stays at the shoulder, the working arm rotates the dumbbell from a supinated position at the chest to a pronated press overhead. The alternating pattern adds core anti-lateral-flexion demand.

en: Sit or stand with a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level.
Start with palms facing your face (supinated grip), elbows tucked in front.
Brace your core hard.
Press the right dumbbell up while rotating your wrist outward to a pronated grip at lockout.
Lock out the right arm overhead while keeping the left dumbbell stationary at the shoulder.
Reverse the motion, rotating back to the supinated grip at the shoulder.
Repeat with the left arm, while the right stays at the shoulder.
Alternate sides with each rep.
Hits all three deltoid heads with the rotation
Adds anti-lateral-flexion core challenge
Single-arm version builds stability
Time-under-tension increased by alternating
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong shoulder development variation

description.en: The dumbbell alternate front raise is a single-joint isolation exercise that targets the anterior (front) head of the deltoid. Standing with a dumbbell in each hand, you lift one dumbbell at a time straight forward to shoulder height. The alternating pattern allows greater focus per arm and exposes left-right imbalances.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your thighs with palms facing your body or facing your thighs.
Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your chest tall.
Set a slight bend in your elbows and lock that angle in throughout the movement.
Lift the dumbbell in your right hand straight forward and up. Rotate your wrist as you lift so your palm faces the floor at the top.
Continue until your right arm is roughly parallel to the floor (at shoulder height). Pause briefly at the top.
Lower the right dumbbell under control over two to three seconds back to your thigh.
As the right dumbbell reaches the bottom, begin lifting the left dumbbell in the same pattern.
Continue alternating arms for the desired number of total reps. Use light to moderate weight; do not swing.
Direct isolation of the anterior deltoid
Alternating pattern allows focused work per arm
Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances
Reduces the temptation to swing both arms together
Easy to do at home with one pair of dumbbells
Useful accessory after compound pressing

description.en: The dumbbell bent over row is a two-arm horizontal pulling exercise where you hinge at the hips and row a dumbbell in each hand simultaneously. The independent dumbbells allow a longer range of motion and a more natural pull path than the barbell version, making it excellent for back development, especially when training at home or with limited equipment.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart and a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body.
Hinge forward at the hips with a slight knee bend until your torso is roughly 45 degrees from horizontal.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down at arm’s length. Brace your core, pull your shoulders down and back, and lock in your back angle.
Row both dumbbells up toward your hips by driving your elbows up and back. Keep your elbows tracking close to your body.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the row.
Pause briefly, then lower the dumbbells under control back to the starting hang position. Feel a stretch in your lats at the bottom.
Maintain the same torso angle throughout the set — do not stand up between reps.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Stand up and rest the dumbbells between sets.
Builds the entire back: lats, rhomboids, traps, rear delts
Longer range of motion than barbell rows
Independent dumbbells expose and correct left-right imbalances
More natural pull path is easier on the shoulders
Strong grip and forearm builder
Works at home with one pair of dumbbells

description.en: The dumbbell deadlift bent over row links a Romanian-style deadlift with a bent over row. After lifting the dumbbells from the floor, you hold the bottom hinge position and perform a row before standing up. The combo trains the posterior chain, lats, and back together in a single rep.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbells on the floor in front of your feet.
Hinge at the hips with a slight knee bend and grip the dumbbells.
Pull the dumbbells up by hinging back to a roughly horizontal torso position.
Hold the bent over position with dumbbells hanging at arms length.
Row both dumbbells up to your lower ribs by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the row.
Lower the dumbbells back down to arms length.
Stand all the way up, then return the dumbbells to the floor for the next rep.
Trains hinge and row patterns in one efficient rep
Builds the entire posterior chain
Develops lat and middle back thickness
Time-efficient compound exercise
Strong grip and forearm involvement
Excellent finisher for back day

description.en: The dumbbell hang power clean and jerk is a variant of the hang clean and jerk where the clean is received in a quarter-squat (power) position rather than a full squat. From the hang position, dumbbells are cleaned to the rack in a power position, then jerked overhead.

en: Stand holding dumbbells at mid-thigh (hang position).
Hinge slightly. Drive your hips forward explosively.
Pull the dumbbells up by shrugging and pulling the elbows high.
Catch the dumbbells at your shoulders in a quarter-squat (power) position.
Stand up from the power catch.
Immediately dip your knees and drive the dumbbells overhead (jerk).
Catch at lockout. Stand tall.
Lower back to hang. Use moderate weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Builds explosive power with power position catch
Less demanding than full squat catch
Combines clean and jerk with dumbbells
Excellent CrossFit movement
Develops bilateral overhead stability
Time-efficient conditioning

description.en: The dumbbell incline around the world arcs two dumbbells from the hip position up to overhead in a wide circular path while lying on an incline bench. The arcing motion hits the chest and front delts through a long range of motion.

en: Lie on an incline bench (30 to 45 degrees). Hold dumbbells at your hips with palms facing up.
Keeping arms mostly straight (slight elbow bend), arc the dumbbells out to the sides and up.
Continue the arc until the dumbbells meet overhead.
Reverse the arc back down to your hips through the same path.
Use light weight — this exercise puts significant demand on the shoulders through the arc.
Move slowly with control.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Feel the stretch and contraction through the entire arc.
Long range of motion for chest and delts
Incline angle emphasizes upper chest
Builds shoulder mobility
Unique arcing stimulus
Old-school bodybuilding exercise
Engages multiple upper body muscles

description.en: The dumbbell incline squeeze press performs a dumbbell press on an incline bench while squeezing the two dumbbells together throughout the movement. The squeeze activates the inner pec fibers and the incline angle targets the upper chest — a double stimulus for upper inner chest development.

en: Set an incline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand.
Press the dumbbells together at your chest. Maintain firm inward pressure.
Press both dumbbells up together to lockout, keeping them in contact the entire time.
Squeeze hard at the top — both the press and the inward squeeze.
Lower under control. Keep squeezing.
Do not let the dumbbells separate at any point.
Use lighter weight than standard incline press due to the squeeze demand.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Targets the upper inner chest
Squeeze activates pec adduction
Incline angle targets clavicular head
Builds chest definition
Engages the triceps heavily
Unique incline press variation

description.en: The dumbbell lying wide grip row on rack is a chest supported row variation with a wide grip. The lifter lies face down on a bench set high enough to clear the dumbbells and rows them up wide with elbows flared. The wide grip targets the upper back hard.

en: Set a flat bench on a power rack at a height that lets the dumbbells clear the floor.
Pick up two dumbbells and lie face down on the bench.
Hold the dumbbells with a wide grip and palms facing the floor.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the dumbbells up wide with elbows flared out.
Drive the elbows back at shoulder height.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back down with control.
Strong upper back builder
No lower back strain
Trains the rear delts
Builds back thickness
Useful back move
Wide grip targets the rhomboids

description.en: The dumbbell one arm wide grip bench press uses a wide arm position with a single dumbbell at a time. Pressing one side of the body creates strong rotational force the core must resist while the wide grip emphasizes the outer chest. The combination builds unilateral chest strength and trunk control.

en: Lie on a flat bench with a single dumbbell in your right hand.
Hold the dumbbell at chest level with your arm wider than shoulder-width.
Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back.
Brace your core hard against the asymmetric load.
Press the dumbbell up to lockout while keeping the left arm relaxed.
Maintain the wide arm position throughout the press.
Lower the dumbbell back to chest level with control.
Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Builds unilateral chest strength
Wide grip emphasizes outer pec
Strong anti-rotation core demand
Corrects left-right imbalances
Time-efficient single-arm work
Useful for breaking through bench plateaus

description.en: The dumbbell single arm preacher curl is performed at a preacher bench with one arm at a time. The single arm pattern allows mind-muscle focus on the working bicep while the preacher pad eliminates body english entirely. It is a strong choice for correcting strength imbalances in the biceps.

en: Sit at a preacher bench with the pad against your right armpit.
Hold a dumbbell in your right hand with an underhand grip.
Drape your right arm over the preacher pad with arm fully extended.
Pin your chest to the pad and brace your core.
Use your left hand to support yourself on the bench.
Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow.
Squeeze the bicep hard at the top.
Lower the dumbbell back down with control to full extension. Switch arms.
Strict single-arm bicep isolation
Eliminates body english
Allows mind-muscle focus on working arm
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong peak contraction
Useful for breaking through bicep plateaus

description.en: The dumbbell step back lunge and row combines two movements into one combo. As you step back into a reverse lunge, you row the dumbbells up to your hips. The combo trains legs and back simultaneously with strong cardiovascular demand. It is a time-efficient compound movement.

en: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Step back with your right leg into a reverse lunge.
As you reach the bottom of the lunge, hinge slightly forward.
Row both dumbbells up to your hips by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the row.
Lower the dumbbells back down to arms length as you stand back up.
Repeat on the other side, alternating legs.
Trains legs and back together
Strong cardiovascular component
Time-efficient compound combo
Builds posterior chain and lat strength
Functional movement pattern
Develops coordination across patterns

description.en: The dumbbell suitcase carry is a unilateral loaded carry where you hold a heavy dumbbell in only one hand and walk for distance. The asymmetric load demands extreme anti-lateral flexion core strength to prevent the body from tilting toward the loaded side. It is one of the most effective oblique and core stability exercises.

en: Place a heavy dumbbell on the floor next to your right foot.
Squat down and grip the dumbbell with your right hand.
Stand up tall, holding the dumbbell at your right side. Keep your left arm relaxed at your side.
Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Resist the urge to lean toward the loaded side. Stand perfectly tall.
Walk forward with controlled, normal-length strides.
Walk for the desired distance (20 to 50 meters) or time.
Switch sides for equal work. Use heavy weight.
Builds elite anti-lateral flexion core stability
Heavily targets the obliques
Develops grip strength
Trains posture under asymmetric load
Excellent for athletes
Time-efficient core builder

description.en: The EZ bar seated close grip shoulder press is a seated overhead press done with a close grip on an EZ curl bar. The narrow grip shifts focus to the triceps while still loading the shoulders. It is a strong shoulder and tricep combo move.

en: Sit upright on a bench with back support.
Hold an EZ curl bar with a close grip at chest height.
Brace your core and keep the back against the support.
Press the bar straight up overhead.
Lock out the elbows at the top.
Squeeze the shoulders and triceps hard.
Lower the bar with control to the chest.
Continue for the working set.
Tricep biased press
Builds the shoulders
Strong overhead move
Useful press variation
Builds the upper arms

description.en: The hack calf raise is a standing calf raise performed on a hack squat machine. You stand on the foot plate with only the balls of your feet on the edge, then raise and lower your heels against the sled resistance. The machine provides back support and allows heavy, progressive calf loading.

en: Stand on the hack squat machine foot plate with only the balls of your feet on the lower edge. Heels hang off.
Position the shoulder pads on your shoulders. Brace your core.
Unlock the safety catches and support the weight with straight legs.
Lower your heels as far as possible for a deep calf stretch.
Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control. Full range of motion on every rep.
Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Allows heavy, progressive calf loading
Back support reduces lower-back stress
Full range of motion with deep stretch
Targets the gastrocnemius (standing position)
Easy to load progressively
Useful when no dedicated calf raise machine is available

description.en: The high knee against wall drill is a sprint mechanics exercise where you lean forward against a wall in the sprint posture and drive your knees up alternately. The wall provides feedback and stability, allowing you to focus purely on hip flexor power and knee drive without balance demand.

en: Stand facing a wall about three to four feet away.
Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height. Lean forward into the wall with your body angled like a sprinter.
Form a straight line from your head through your shoulders, hips, and ankle (only your front leg touches the floor).
Begin driving your knees up alternately like a sprint stride — knee height to hip level or higher.
Push off through the ball of your foot with each step.
Maintain the forward lean against the wall throughout.
Pump knees rapidly. Aim for fast turnover and high knees.
Perform for 15 to 30 seconds per set.
Trains sprint mechanics and knee drive
Builds hip flexor power
Wall provides feedback for proper sprint posture
Removes balance demand to isolate leg drive
No equipment needed beyond a wall
Used by track and field athletes

description.en: The hollow rock is a foundational gymnastics core exercise where you hold a hollow body position (slightly rounded back, ribs down, legs and arms extended) and rock back and forth like a rocking chair. It builds tremendous anterior core strength and is the foundation for many advanced gymnastics skills.

en: Lie on your back. Press your lower back firmly into the floor.
Lift your shoulders, arms, head, and legs slightly off the floor.
Reach your arms overhead alongside your ears. Keep your legs straight and pointed.
Round your upper back slightly. Pull your ribs down toward your hips. This is the hollow position — your body forms a gentle banana shape.
Brace your core hard. Maintain this position rigidly throughout the rocking.
Begin gently rocking back and forth like a rocking chair, using a slight upper-body lift to drive the rock.
Keep the hollow shape constant — the entire body moves as one unit. Do not break the position.
Continue for 20 to 60 seconds. If you cannot maintain the hollow shape, regress to the hollow hold first.
Builds elite anterior core strength
Foundational gymnastics movement
Teaches rigid core bracing
Carries over to all advanced calisthenics skills
No equipment needed
Develops body control and awareness

description.en: The kettlebell seesaw press holds two KBs in the front rack and alternates pressing them in a seesaw pattern — as one goes up, the other comes down. The continuous alternating pattern builds shoulder endurance and core anti-lateral flexion while keeping constant tension on the shoulders.

en: Clean two KBs to the front rack position.
Press the right KB overhead.
As the right KB reaches lockout, begin lowering it while simultaneously pressing the left KB up.
The two bells move in opposite directions — one up, one down.
Continue in a smooth seesaw rhythm.
Maintain upright posture. Brace core throughout.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per arm.
Move with control and rhythm.
Continuous shoulder tension through alternating pattern
Builds shoulder endurance
Develops core anti-lateral flexion
Time-efficient pressing variation
Builds coordination and timing
Engaging movement pattern

description.en: Push-up with chair uses a sturdy chair for either incline push-ups (hands on the chair seat — easier) or decline push-ups (feet on the chair seat — harder). It adjusts difficulty using common household furniture.

en: For incline (easier): Place hands on the chair seat. Feet on the floor. Perform push-ups.
For decline (harder): Place feet on the chair seat. Hands on the floor. Perform push-ups.
Ensure the chair is stable and will not slide. Use a wall behind the chair.
Maintain a straight body line throughout.
Lower your chest toward the chair (incline) or floor (decline).
Press back up.
Incline targets less chest load; decline targets more upper chest.
Aim for 10 to 20 reps.
Adjustable difficulty with common furniture
No gym equipment needed
Incline is beginner-friendly
Decline targets upper chest
Easy to set up at home
Progressive by switching from incline to decline

description.en: The rear shift lunge from deficit is a reverse lunge variation done from a raised platform. The front foot stays on the deficit, and the lifter steps back into a lunge to deepen the range. It loads the quads and glutes through a longer range than flat ground.

en: Stand on a low platform or weight plate.
Set the feet hip width apart on the deficit.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Step one foot back off the platform.
Lower the back knee toward the floor.
Stop just above the floor with the front shin near vertical.
Drive through the front foot to return to the platform.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Loads the front leg
Longer range than flat
Builds the quads
Strong lunge variation
Trains the glutes
Useful for balance

description.en: The resistance band 45 degrees hyperextension adds resistance to a 45 degree hyperextension. The lifter loops a band over the shoulders and anchors it low, then performs the hyperextension on a 45 degree bench. The band loads the back extensors and glutes hard.

en: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point.
Loop the other end across the upper back behind the neck.
Set up on a 45 degree hyperextension bench.
Hook the heels under the foot pads and the hips against the pad.
Brace your core and start with the torso angled down.
Extend the hips lifting the torso to a straight line with the body.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Lower the torso back down with control.
Strong posterior chain builder
Adds resistance to back extension
Builds the glutes
Useful back move
Strong band move
Builds the hamstrings

description.en: The reverse-grip machine lat pulldown is a vertical pulling exercise performed with an underhand (supinated) grip on a lat pulldown machine. The grip places the biceps in a stronger position and shifts emphasis to the lower lats and lower trapezius, providing a different stimulus than the standard overhand pulldown. It is an excellent variation for full lat development.

en: Set up the lat pulldown machine with a straight bar attachment. Adjust the thigh pad to lock your legs in firmly.
Reach up and grip the bar with an underhand (palms-toward-you) grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Sit down with your thighs locked under the pad. Sit upright with chest tall.
Brace your core, pull your shoulder blades down and back, and slightly arch your upper back.
Pull the bar down by driving your elbows down and back toward your hips. Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides.
Bring the bar to your upper chest. Squeeze your lats and lower traps at the bottom.
Slowly let the bar travel back up under control until your arms are fully extended. Feel the stretch in your lats.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Strict form matters more than load on this lift.
Biases the lower lats and lower trapezius more than overhand pulldowns
Heavily recruits the biceps as a secondary mover
Often easier on the shoulders than wide-grip variations
Shorter pull path lets you load heavier than overhand pulldowns for many lifters
Builds back thickness as well as width
Excellent variation in a complete back program

description.en: The reverse plank is an isometric core exercise where you face up, supporting your body on your hands and heels with your body in a straight line from head to heels. It strengthens the posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, lower back) and rear shoulder stabilizers while stretching the chest and hip flexors. It is the opposite of a standard front plank.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front of you. Place your hands flat on the floor behind your hips, fingers pointing toward your feet.
Press through your hands and heels to lift your hips off the floor. Your body should form a straight line from your head to your heels.
Squeeze your glutes and hamstrings hard. Point your toes forward.
Pull your shoulders down and back. Open your chest. Look straight ahead or slightly up.
Do not let your hips sag. Maintain the straight body line throughout the hold.
Hold for the desired duration — aim for 20 to 60 seconds per set.
To finish, lower your hips back to the floor under control.
If the full version is too difficult, start with a reverse tabletop (knees bent at 90 degrees).
Strengthens the posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, lower back)
Stretches the chest and hip flexors
Builds rear shoulder stability
Counterbalances the dominance of front-plank and push-up training
Improves posture by strengthening upper-back extensors
No equipment needed — works anywhere

description.en: The roll around the world lying on floor is a comprehensive upper body release drill. Lying on a foam roller and shifting the body in a circular pattern releases the lats, mid back, obliques, and rear delts in one sequence.

en: Lie on the back with a foam roller under the upper back.
Bend the knees with feet flat on the floor.
Brace the core and lift the hips slightly.
Roll the upper back across the roller.
Shift to one side to roll the lat.
Continue around to roll the obliques.
Work back through the mid back and other lat.
Continue circular rolling for the working time.
Releases the upper back.
Mobilizes the lats and obliques.
Comprehensive upper body release.
Useful for recovery.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll forearms standing against wall is a self myofascial release drill done with a foam roller pinned vertically against a wall. Pressing the forearm into the roller and moving up and down releases tightness from heavy gripping and computer work.

en: Stand facing a wall with a foam roller pinned vertically against it.
Place one forearm flat against the roller.
Press the arm into the roller with the body weight.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Slide the forearm slowly up and down the roller.
Rotate the wrist to cover all sides of the forearm.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the forearms.
Reduces grip fatigue.
Improves wrist mobility.
Useful for climbers and lifters.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The side wrist pull stretch is a standing stretch where you reach one arm overhead, grasp the wrist with the opposite hand, and pull to the side. It deeply stretches the lat, obliques, and side body of the reaching arm — providing a deeper stretch than a standard side bend.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Reach your right arm straight up overhead.
Grasp your right wrist with your left hand.
Use your left hand to pull your right arm slightly to the left, while bending your torso to the left.
Combine the side bend with the wrist pull to deepen the stretch.
Feel the deep stretch through your right lat, obliques, and side body.
Keep both feet planted. Do not lean forward or backward.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply. Switch sides.
Deep lat and side body stretch
Improves lateral spinal flexibility
Combines side bend with wrist pull for greater depth
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Excellent post-workout stretch

description.en: The sit up with arms on chest is a regression of the standard sit up done with the arms folded across the chest. Removing the arm swing eliminates momentum and forces the abs and hip flexors to do all the work.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Cross the arms over the chest.
Brace the core and keep the chin tucked slightly.
Lift the upper body up off the floor.
Continue lifting until the elbows reach the thighs.
Squeeze the abs hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Continue for the working set.
Builds the abs.
Trains the hip flexors.
Hands on chest removes momentum.
Bodyweight move.
Useful for core size.

description.en: The Smith reverse grip press uses an underhand (supinated) grip on the Smith machine bar during a bench press. The reverse grip targets the upper pec while the Smith fixed path eliminates balance demands. The combination is a strong upper chest specialization variation that is shoulder-friendly.

en: Set up a flat bench under the Smith machine bar.
Lie back with eyes under the bar.
Grip the bar with palms facing you (underhand grip), shoulder-width apart.
Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back.
Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists.
Lower the bar with control to your upper chest.
Press the bar back up by squeezing the upper chest.
Re-rack the bar by rotating your wrists when finished.
Targets upper chest fibers
Reduces front delt involvement
Smith fixed bar path eliminates balance demands
Less shoulder strain than pronated grip
Useful for chest specialization
Strong tricep engagement

description.en: The standing calf raise with support is a basic calf raise that uses a wall or sturdy support for balance. The lifter focuses purely on the calf raise without worrying about balance. It is a useful introductory calf builder.

en: Stand facing a wall or sturdy support.
Place the hands on the support at chest height.
Set the feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and keep the legs straight.
Press up onto the balls of the feet.
Squeeze the calves hard at the top.
Lower with control to the floor.
Continue for the working set.
Builds the calves
Easy balance
Useful for beginners
No equipment needed
Strong calf basic

description.en: The suspender arm curl is performed gripping suspension straps with an underhand grip, then curling your body up by bending only at the elbows. The bodyweight loading on the biceps is easy to scale by changing your foot position. It is a strong choice for bicep training without weights.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Stand facing the anchor and grip the handles with palms facing up (underhand grip).
Walk your feet forward so your body angles back with arms extended.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart on the floor.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Curl your body up toward the handles by bending only at the elbows.
Keep your upper arms locked in front of your body throughout.
Lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
Bodyweight bicep training
Easy to scale by changing foot position
Builds bicep size with no weights
Excellent for home or travel training
Strong forearm engagement
Constant strap tension

description.en: The suspension underhand grip inverted row is a TRX row with a supinated underhand grip. The grip biases the biceps and lower lats more than the standard grip. It is a strong upper body builder using just bodyweight and TRX straps.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles with palms facing up in an underhand grip.
Walk the feet forward until the body leans back at an angle.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the chest up toward the handles by bending the elbows.
Drive the elbows down past the body.
Squeeze the lats and biceps hard. Lower back to the start with control.
Strong unilateral back builder
Underhand grip biases biceps
Trains lower lats
Strong TRX move
Useful pull up progression
Builds the back

description.en: The toy soldier dynamic stretch is a walking warm-up drill where you kick one straight leg up toward the opposite outstretched hand with each step — like a soldier marching with stiff legs. It dynamically stretches the hamstrings and hip flexors while building coordination.

en: Stand tall with feet together. Extend your left arm straight forward at shoulder height.
Take a step forward and kick your right (straight) leg up toward your left hand.
Try to touch your toe to your hand or as high as your flexibility allows. Keep the kicking leg straight.
Lower your right foot and step forward. Extend your right arm forward.
Kick your left (straight) leg up toward your right hand.
Continue alternating, walking forward with each kick.
Move with control — do not use momentum to force the kicks higher.
Perform 10 to 15 kicks per leg as part of a dynamic warm-up.
Dynamically stretches the hamstrings
Activates the hip flexors and quadriceps
Builds coordination and balance
Excellent dynamic warm-up before running or lower-body training
No equipment needed
Increases hamstring range of motion over time

description.en: The weighted lying neck extension is a direct neck extensor builder. The lifter lies face down on a bench with the head off the edge and a weight plate held on the back of the head. The lifter extends the neck up to lift the head against the weight.

en: Lie face down on a bench with the head and shoulders off the edge.
Hold a small weight plate on the back of the head with both hands.
Brace your core and let the head hang down.
Extend the neck up lifting the head against the plate.
Continue lifting until the head is in line with the body.
Squeeze the back of the neck at the top.
Pause briefly at the contracted position.
Lower the head back down with control.
Strong neck builder
Builds rear neck size
Useful for athletes
Builds neck strength
Strong neck move
Useful for combat sports
